description_ru: Маршрутка по горным дорогам Грузии, средневековые башни, тосты тамады и деревня Ушгули у подножия ледников.
text:
The minibus from Zugdidi to Mestia, in the mountains of northern Georgia, has no timetable in any sense that a European would recognise. It leaves when it is full. It is full when the driver, a moustachioed man called Levan, decides that it is. For the first hour I was irritated; for the second I was enchanted, because the road had begun to climb into the gorge of the Enguri river, and every bend revealed another ridge of white peaks, closer and more improbable than the last. By the third hour I was no longer thinking about the timetable at all.

Svaneti is one of the most remote regions in the Caucasus, a high, isolated country of snowy passes and deep valleys. For centuries, its people, the Svans, lived in near-independence, protected by geography and by a ferocious code of honour that included, until fairly recently, the blood feud. The visible legacy of that history is the towers. In nearly every village, dozens of slender medieval stone towers rise above the roofs, each about twenty-five metres tall, built so that families could retreat into them when a neighbouring clan attacked. Seen from a distance, with the mountains behind them, they resemble a forest of stone chimneys, or the remains of some enormous, interrupted chess game.

In Mestia, the regional capital, the towers are the first thing you notice and the last thing you forget. Once a remote hamlet, the town has recently been smartened up, with a new airstrip, cobbled lanes and a number of boutique hotels, yet it has not lost its character. My guesthouse was run by a woman called Nana, who greeted me with a glass of homemade wine, a plate of cheese and a suspicion, which I soon learned to recognise, that I was too thin. In the Caucasus, hospitality is a form of moral duty, and a guest who declines food is considered to have committed a minor offence.

Dinner that night was a lesson in the subject. A Georgian meal is organised around the supra, a feast presided over by a toastmaster known as the tamada, who proposes a series of formal toasts in a fixed order, to peace, to ancestors, to the dead, to children, to absent friends, each accompanied by a speech and a swallow of wine. Nana's husband, a retired mountain guide, took the role of tamada, and spoke with such eloquence in Georgian that, although I understood not a word, I found myself near to tears at the toast to the dead. The food kept arriving: khachapuri, the bread boat filled with cheese; kubdari, a spiced meat pie that is a Svan speciality; and a bowl of salt flavoured with garlic, marigold and fenugreek, called svanuri marili, which is wickedly good on everything.

The next morning, I joined a driver for the long, jolting ride to Ushguli, a cluster of four villages at around 2,100 metres that is often described as one of the highest continuously inhabited settlements in Europe. The road, which is partly unpaved, climbs through a landscape of alpine meadows, and at one point my driver stopped to let a herd of cows complete a leisurely crossing. Cows are, in the Svan highlands, the real arbiters of traffic. At the end of the road, beneath the glaciers of Mount Shkhara, which at 5,193 metres is among the highest peaks in Georgia, I found a village that looked as if it had been plucked from the twelfth century and dropped, with some tenderness, among the wildflowers.

I spent two days there, walking up the valley to the foot of the glacier, where the Enguri begins as a grey, furious trickle. On the way I met a man mowing a steep meadow with a scythe, a woman carrying a bundle of hay on her back, and a pair of boys who followed me for half a mile, shouting the only English they knew, which was the name of a famous footballer. Everywhere, there was a feeling of continuity, of people whose lives had been shaped by altitude and snow, and who were slightly bemused by the idea that anyone should travel so far to look at it.

The challenges of the region are real. Winters are long and cut off many villages for weeks, and the young drift away to Tbilisi or abroad in search of work. Tourism has brought welcome income, but also anxiety about what it may do to the culture it celebrates. A guesthouse owner in Ushguli told me, with a shrug, that she did not know whether she was a custodian or a museum exhibit. I thought it the most honest sentence I heard on the whole trip.

On my last evening, I climbed a hillside above Mestia with a flask of tea. The sun slipped behind the peak of Ushba, which has two jagged summits like the horns of an animal, and the towers below me turned from grey to rose. Somewhere, a dog barked and was answered. Smoke rose from chimneys in thin, straight lines. It was, I realised, the first time in months that I had not reached for my phone, and I did not miss it.

Levan was waiting at the bus stop the next morning, and gave me a look of mild reproach, as if I were leaving before dessert. "You come back," he said, which was not a request. I told him I would. For once in my travelling life, I intended to keep my word.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение: hospiˈtality, contiˈnuity, imˈprobable. В hospitality главное ударение на -tal-.
Краткое «ʊ» — губы слегка округлены, звук короче русского «у»: good, looked.
«v» — верхние зубы касаются нижней губы, голос включён: valley, village.
Связывайте слова: a_bowl_of звучит как «э-боул-оф» без паузы.

questions.question: How does the minibus to Mestia work?
questions.answer: It has no timetable and leaves when it is full.

questions.question: What are the towers in Svaneti for?
questions.answer: Families retreated into them when attacked by other clans.

questions.question: What is a tamada?
questions.answer: The toastmaster who presides over a Georgian feast.

questions.question: What did the guesthouse owner in Ushguli say?
questions.answer: She did not know whether she was a custodian or a museum exhibit.
